newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks progress, session set for Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks progress, session set for Wednesday.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

State attorneys general and cigarette makers made progress Tuesday in efforts to reach a settlement to resolve mounting litigation against the tobacco industry and agreed to continue negotiations Wednesday.
The attorneys general had said earlier Tuesday they would end talks in the afternoon if they did not feel tobacco representatives were open to their proposals.

"I have said that the day we don't make progress ... I'm leaving. And we're coming back tomorrow," said Washington Attorney General Christine Gregoire following a session with cigarette makers that ended in the early evening.
"We exchanged a lot of ideas today ... proposals and counterproposals," said Richard Scruggs, a lawyer aiding Mississippi and other states.

The attorneys general have sued the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. The negotiations also include representatives of the health community and plaintiffs lawyers representing smokers.

The parties maintain that a jury verdict in favor of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. in a trial in Jacksonville, Fla., on Monday would not affect their negotiations. Two of the plaintiffs lawyers in that case, Norwood "Woody" Wilner and Ronald Motley joined negotiations on Tuesday.
"Things look good. We're making progress but it's incremental at this point ... we're taking baby steps," said Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore after an early morning session with colleagues.
The key issues being discussed are civil liability and public health, including efforts aimed at reducing underage smoking.
Moore said the state lawyers were organized into five working groups to consider separate issues, including whether there is insurance to cover claims against the industry.
The attorneys general have suggested several proposals to the tobacco industry over the past few days on how to deal with the difficult issue of liability.
The states want to give the industry an incentive to settle, but refuse to agree to blanket protection from all lawsuits.
"Immunity, that word isn't even in our vocabulary," Moore said.
One negotiator told Reuters that one of the proposals would set up a fund with an annual limit, which would allow the industry to know how much to set aside each year.

If a smoker is successful in a lawsuit against the industry and the fund for that year is low or already has been exhausted, the plaintiff would still get paid, but the full amount might not be received until the following year, the source said.
"This is just one of the proposals. There are other things on the table," he said.
Florida Attorney General Robert Butterworth said the tobacco industry also was looking for a way to eliminate or reduce the possibility of punitive damages.
"I am personally opposed to a cap (on damages). If it is too low, it denies access to the courts," Butterworth said.
Gregoire said the parties are not discussing potential criminal actions. No federal authorities or congressmen are involved in the negotiations.
"The only people here are the people that have filed lawsuits," she said.

The Justice Department is currently investigating the tobacco industry on allegations that include the possibility that manufacturers lied or withheld information from federal agencies about nicotine and addiction and other health risks.
In Jacksonville, Fla., a jury Monday cleared R.J. Reynolds of responsibility for the death of a smoker who died of lung cancer.

The jury deliberated for eight hours over two days before deciding Reynolds had neither acted negligently nor made a dangerous, defective product that caused the death of Jean Connor, who smoked heavily from the time she was a teenager and died of lung cancer in October 1995 at age 49.

Despite the verdict, tobacco company stocks were lower Tuesday after gaining sharply on Monday. RJR lost $2.375 to $30.25, and Philip Morris was off $2.375 at $41.75, both in heavy trading on the New York Stock Exchange. In contrast, Loews Corp. gained $1 to $96.625, also on the NYSE.
